Beyond 12: The Harmonic


Universe of 24-TET


jiia Prikhodko


Beyond 12: The Harmonic Universe of 24-TET


Ilia Prikhodko 2026

‌Annotation


What if the musical system we take for granted is only a fraction of something larger? What if there is a whole world tucked between C and C-sharp — one that composers have so far left untouched?

This book is an invitation into that world. It is about 24-tone equal temperament (24-TET), and it lays out a working modal system that pushes

past the limits of classical diatonicism — one you can start experimenting with

before the theory is fully built.

Together with the author, you will travel from your first hesitant steps across twenty-four notes to a coherent tonal structure: rediscovering the laws of music theory for twice the number of pitches, meeting ultra-chromaticism up close, absorbing new patterns of tension and key kinship — and seeing how music-making actually works beyond the familiar twelve-step grid.

This is not a textbook, nor a reference work in the usual sense. It is an investigation in which the reader becomes a co-author: listening, testing, getting it wrong, and finding it — alongside the author. The book shows that even in a world where everything seems to have been discovered already, there is still room for a personal discovery — and it hands you the tools to make one.


Figured-bass is the whole foundation of the music, and is played with both hands in such a manner that the left hand plays the notes written down, while the right adds in consonances or dissonances, the result being an agreeable harmony to the glory of God and justifiable gratification of the senses; for the sole end and aim of general-bass, like that of all music, should be nothing else than God’s glory and pleasant recreations. Where this object is not kept in view there can be no true music, but an infernal scraping and bawling.


— Johann Sebastian Bach

‌Chapter 1

A Cast of Diatonicism in Quarter-Tone Space


Today, in November 2026, I can no longer say with any certainty that every child gets their first taste of music by poking at the white keys of a piano at home. But this beautiful, inspiring cliché is begging to open a chapter devoted to diatonicism. So let’s imagine we are five again, our fingers running across the keys on their own. The notes pour out like a little stream, and we could not care less that we are, at this very moment, telling a story woven from a mixture of modes within a single key. Or maybe several keys — assuming we didn’t skip music school. But with absolute, reinforced-concrete certainty, we have no access to the mathematical model behind this scale. And we don’t need it: we aren’t planning to change anything, we’re perfectly happy, the sun is shining through the window, and life is beautiful when you can just sit down at an instrument.

I’m 38 now, and I didn’t have a childhood like that. In front of me is Ableton with a quarter-tone tuning, Pianoteq where a minimally acceptable sound comes without any extra hassle, a self-taught background, and my own view of what’s happening in music — and outside the window. So let’s try trans-posing diatonicism onto twice the number of notes and see what discoveries it leads us to.

24-TET began to attract serious attention from music enthusiasts in the early twentieth century. Since then, and right up to the present day, it has remained something of an undiscovered curiosity — a window of possibilities, and a bit like a Rubik’s Cube: it fascinates, it disappoints you quickly, and it leaves you knowing the ending (”surely something beautiful can come out of this”) without having the faintest idea of the method.

It is not surprising, then, that building a general theoretical framework for it may seem like an overambitious task — one that would retrace, for 24-tone temperament, the entire path music theory and practice have spent centuries laying down for the twelve-tone system: from intervals and chords to func-tions, voice leading, and notation — only this time with a step half as wide and a quarter-tone hierarchy to account for. But that is exactly why it is worth trying.

Diatonicism in its familiar twelve-tone form is built on simple and reliable laws. The fifth generator (7 semitones) and the octave (12 semitones) set up a coordinate system of intervals — a coherent system with a simple algorithm that lets a listener identify a scale degree by its sounding pitch in real time, right as the music plays (it comes through especially clearly in classical music). The core of diatonicism is seven consecutive notes along the circle of fifths.

The tonic — the root of this core — is defined by context: by its position in the musical phrase, and by the minimal set of notes that unambiguously points to the tonal center.

The octave is a cognitive interval that establishes an equivalence relation: notes an octave apart are heard as ”the same.” Without octave equivalence, the system of notes would be infinite. Functional harmony in diatonicism is narrative: we leave home (the tonic), make our way, and return to our place.

The classic progression tonic–subdominant–dominant–tonic defines

a segment with two fixed points at either end.

Taking up our handy Rubik’s Cube analogy, we can picture 24-TET as a higher-order combinatorial apparatus in which we see, first, two 12-TET subsystems separated from each other by 50 cents, and second, previously unseen variants of familiar intervals. And the main discovery is that three versions of the tritone exist in 24-TET:


  • Pure tritone — 12 quarter-tones (600 cents). In 12-TET, this is the only tritone (6 semitones).

  • Augmented tritone — 13 quarter-tones (650 cents).

  • Diminished tritone — 11 quarter-tones (550 cents).


Figure 1.1: 24-TET octave

At this point I owe you a reference to three mathematical papers I wrote under the influence of works by distinguished music-theorist-mathematicians. With several of them, I had the honor of exchanging brief correspondence, and I am grateful for their feedback. I leave the current versions of the papers in the appendix so that the book doesn’t sprawl in all directions right now and I can continue a minimally assembled narrative. Any hypothetical criticism inherent to this topic is welcome and will be analyzed as time permits. But right now, an important clarification: of the three tritone variants, particular significance belongs to the reciprocally inverse tritone generator — the pair

{+11, +13}. As it turns out, it ”glues” the two subsystems into one. Let’s find

out how.

What distinguishes a mode from a trivial or chaotic collection of notes?

Patterned intervallic organization.



Figure 1.2: Major scale in 24-TET


In diatonicism (12-TET), there are two types of patterns. The horizon-tal pattern — the intervals between adjacent scale degrees. For major, it looks like [4, 4, 2, 4, 4, 4, 2] in quarter-tones. The vertical pattern — the in-tervals between every other degree (e.g. thirds); it emerges as a conse-quence of the horizontal one and shows which triads form within the scale: [8, 6, 6, 8, 8, 6, 6].

Both the horizontal and vertical patterns change from mode to mode, but they preserve the structure of alternation. This gives us the criterion by which diatonicism can be described.

The question arises: can we build an analogous modal architecture in 24-

TET?



Figure 1.3: 10-note mode in 24-TET


In 24-TET, between the 12-TET semitone (2 quarter-tones) and the 12-TET whole tone (4 quarter-tones) there appears a new degree — 3 quarter-tones. If we alternate 3 and 2 in the order 3-2-3-2-3-3-2-3-2, we get a ten-note set.

This mode has a curious symmetry: a shift of 13 maps the first half

(0, 3, 5, 8, 10) onto the second (13, 16, 18, 21, 23).

Even more striking is the vertical pattern: intervals between degrees five positions apart go up by 13 (0 → 13, 3 → 16, 5 → 18, 8 → 21, 10 → 23) —

or, modulo 24, down by 11.

So from the tonic 0 you can rise by 13 quarter-tones to note 13 — or descend by 11 quarter-tones (modulo 24) to the same note. This already resembles the quintal-quartal generator of 12-TET, which likewise shapes the sound of diatonicism.


Figure 1.4: Diatonics reimagined

Unfortunately, this is where the wonders of the mode end: steps of 3 and 2 are too close in size, so the mode sounds monotonous — all degrees are functionally indistinguishable. Ten-note modes of 24-TET are described in the literature; I have examined this mode in detail for its capacity to organize tonal space, and have come to the conclusion that it serves as a theoretical justification for merging the two 12-TETs — a merging that finally occurs if we replace each adjacent pair of steps 2 and 3 with their sum (5).

Having done this, we find ourselves in a space that almost coincides with diatonicism. The only difference is that the alternation carries us from the 12-TET of ”even” degrees into the 12-TET of ”odd” degrees — shifted by half a step; and the pattern still fails to close into an octave, moving through the notes in a peculiar mathematical order.

But we do have a clear path through the octaves that does not contradict how the brain processes pitch.

Everything’s by the book — we can breathe again and simply listen, get-ting used to the new sound.

But, hand on heart, does it sound harmonious? Something is clearly missing.

‌Chapter 2


Tritonics. Shaping a New Sound


Three quarter-tones. Three variants of the tritone. What else might we add? Three tonics?


Two tonics — one in each of the two 12-TET subsystems — are already there, and together they sound the way they sound; it’s time to move on and give ourselves over to experimentation. What else are we missing for the full set?


So far, we have been locked into the standard logic of modal construction. We have made some progress, and we can now say with confidence that the two merged 12-TET systems sound almost as coherent as a plain major scale. Still, it’s hard to fully get used to that dry sound — it just sounds too mathematical. And we have one small problem left to solve: octave closure. Until we fix that, the paths to registral motion, modulation, and the other joys of professional composition remain closed to us.


Speaking of composers: it’s no secret that the greats didn’t pull their works out of thin air. They spent years soaking in the sound of scales, studying counterpoint, and finding their own techniques that opened up new sounds — passing the baton to the next generation. Tonal music has evolved through chromaticism: from the birth of major and minor to their complete dissolution into all twelve notes.


But how do we give every note a chance to sound in 24-TET?

Figure 2.1: 24-TET Tritonics

Hello, ultra-chromaticism — anything that goes beyond twelve semitones. Even at a glance, this massive triangle draws the eye: crisp sequences of thirds, fourths, and tritones, already dressed in triads and seventh chords. Our Rubik’s Cube is taking shape — and becoming available for a full theo-retical analysis. Now, on this peculiar ladder of 25 positions (0…24), despite the abundance of notes, we can for the first time feel the coherence of the sound, truly hear the motion of voices and, at last, the long-awaited tenden-cies. What is especially striking is how closely the first eight degrees of the mode resemble the major scale — but what comes next?


The motion clearly continues, and new stable degrees are waiting for us to reach them; but at some point it becomes harder and harder to get there, the tension between the notes builds to alpine proportions, and while listening to the last degrees there arises a perfectly natural urge to cut the highs — in the literal and figurative sense.


Well, then: let’s start trimming the degrees, discarding the upper ones starting from the eighth, and at some point we arrive at three fully formed micro-scales that sound like a sequence of major, minor, and Locrian within a single octave — with a leading-tone cadence into the tonic on the 23rd degree. Wow.

Figure 2.2: 24-TET micro-scales


You can’t just wave away a structure like that, call it sound-design hack-work or a fake. If it sounds like a duck, it’s a duck. Shall we go on? Of course, every degree gives rise to its own micro-scales, each with its own pattern and its own sound; it’s not even surprising that they can be grouped into seven modal families (hello, micro-mixolydian). Let’s suppose all of this is serious, and that by pulling the right thread we have unwound the entire ball of 24-TET tonality. But still, we’d like more rules. Where do we get the instruction manual?

There is no manual yet — there are three of my mathematical papers in which I tried to build one. My first attempt at an analogue of the circle of fifths in 24-TET resulted in a mathematical paper on the Harmonic Compass. Later, in the paper on the Harmonic Lattice (and there was also one about the Sphere, with terms borrowed from driving-school manuals and a prediction of cadences), the Compass was supplemented with its realization as an algebraic operator.



Figure 2.3: The Harmonic Compass


To explain it in two sentences: the notes of the modes fit neatly into adjacent pairs of the Compass, which are themselves mobile and depend on the periods of the full 24-note cycle. The main rule that shapes the modes is the switch

from the even to the odd subsystem in the course of motion through chord progressions. Let’s take this as the strict rule of voice leading in 24-TET, and everything else as free style. The details are in the papers; what matters here is that the Compass provides a coordinate system in which modes stop being a random collection of notes.


The next possible steps in tonal space obey a strict, childlike rule: ”What if?”



Figure 2.4: diatonic extension to 5


Figure 2.5: diatonic extension to 7


Figure 2.6: diatonic extension to 9


Figure 2.7: diatonic extension to 11

You might have noticed that our patterns (3-5-3, 5-9-5, and so on) are not random. In mathematical music theory, there is a concept called Maximally Even sets. In simple terms, it’s a way of distributing notes so that they are spaced as evenly as possible from one another. It turns out that in 24-TET, a near-perfect evenness is achieved not by a single generator, but by a specific pairing of odd steps — in our case, the alternation between two different odd degrees (like +3 and +5). This is why our Tritonic system isn’t just one possible variant, but a mathematically grounded result for anyone who wants to pre-serve diatonic logic in a doubled pitch space. The combinatorics of alternating even and odd degrees is mesmerizing. And it’s quite likely that a harmonic filling of larger structures — similar to what we’ve already discovered within a single octave — can be achieved simply by recreating this three-phase flow of harmony inside the structure.



Figure 2.8: Three-phase integration of diatonicism and chromaticism


The number three — three quarter-tones — now stands as the fundamen-tal period that generates the new sound. So I thought: perhaps, when step-ping out of ultra-chromaticism to the next level up, we might once again take it as our guidepost?

What if we have just gained access to boundless combinatorial possibilities for building modes in 24-TET?


Figure 2.9: micro-scales

‌Chapter 3

A General Theory of Music


Since music theory in 24-tone space is being worked out empirically — right now, as it happens (anyone can open a program and start trying out notes in a piano roll) — and since I’m up for adding new stuff to my own previously published papers, I’ve decided to treat this chapter the same way. First, I’ll briefly outline the principles of notation. Then, as my understanding evolves, I’ll keep adding new thoughts on how to compose in 24-TET and what rules are worth following.

From the very beginning of exploring the 24 notes within a single octave, I realized that numbers are the most optimal way to define them. In 12-TET, interval inversions can still be logically packed and internalized while keep-ing letter notation in mind. In 24-TET, that task becomes impossible. Four variants of familiar letters per octave — further complicated by being split into two 12-TET subsystems with both their own and shared rules — simply stop making sense. Numbers, on the other hand, act as ideal logical anchors. It’s easy to attach intervals to them, they divide elegantly into even and odd degrees, and, of course, they are made for mathematical analysis.

The alternation of even degrees (the first 12-TET) and odd degrees (the second 12-TET) is fundamental to shaping this new sound. Automatically, any chord built on even degrees will contain even note numbers — and vice versa for odd ones. Of course, they can include notes from the ”wrong” par-ity to add a touch of wolf fifths, donkey tones, or the sound of failing brake pads, depending on the register. But things aren’t so black and white. We already have historical examples of mixing notes from different subsystems

— modern composers loved the minor third, some called it ”blue” in reference to jazz. In the upper registers, these cross-parity notes produce fascinating, sweeping timbres rather than just harsh dissonances. It all depends on how you use them.

As for the sound of the micro-scales, I found it a good idea to invert the chords of the odd degrees so that the bass note moves up an octave. This rule of the octave lets progressions breathe: the degrees sound like reflections of each other, and you achieve that sought-after harmonic quality.



Figure 3.1: The Rule of the Octave


The three-phase harmonic motion across all 24 degrees within a single oc-tave — which worked out so well earlier — provides a foundation for further analysis and attempts to expand upon it. Right now, we stand at a fork in the road: we can either dig deeper into building a theoretical base for these micro-scales, or push forward and experiment with upper structures. Classi-cal or jazz? It seems we can mix them.

The classical octave frame expands through a simple trick. If we look at the top notes of the micro-scale, they follow the pattern 3-5-3-3-3-5-3. If we then take that same micro-scale and position it not on a standard chromatic layout (0-1-2-3…), but on the degrees of that very pattern (0-3-8-11-14-17-22-1), the top notes will now follow the pattern 5-9-5-5-5-9-5.


And so on, progressively. If we map it onto these new degrees, the top notes become 7-13-7-7-7-13-7. It’s a form of harmonic inflation. By placing the sequence of degree-chords onto the pattern of their top notes, we extend the sound of the micro-scales within the limits of our piano roll. The images of diatonic extensions in the previous section are exactly what you get at the tops of the chords when you run this experiment.


Building progressions is limited only by the number and quality of your ideas. If you’re willing, you can construct a progression within the Tritonic system that includes a ninth chord on the first degree, a tenth chord on the second, eleventh chords on the third and fourth, a twelfth chord on the fifth, a thirteenth chord on the sixth, and fourteenth chords on the seventh and eighth — all so that it sounds like a scale carrying the functional harmony of diatonicism.

Figure 3.2: Upper Structures

It would be plainly wrong to say that Tritonics is an alternative to, or a replacement for, the familiar diatonic sound in 24-TET. Suffice it to recall that beyond diatonic modes and chromaticism, there are pentatonic, octatonic, whole-tone scales, and other experimental structures that have proven their aesthetic beauty and sonic power. The real beauty lies in the possibility of in-tegrating all possible scales with Tritonics within the 24-TET grid. Meanwhile, theoretical questions remain unresolved and require analysis — specifically, regarding the number of new tonalities and the ways to modulate between them. The wave-like sound of transitions between even and odd degrees may be the key to understanding the laws of voice leading and proper orchestra-tion that amplify this effect.

Thus, the core principle of composing in 24-TET is the balance between the two 12-TET subsystems. Like a tightrope walker on a thin rope (where the principle of walking is adapted to extreme conditions), anyone seeking an acceptable sound without dissonances will maintain that necessary balance for artistic purposes.

The Harmonic Compass: Four Self-Dual Unidirectional Cycles in 24-Tone Equal Temperament

Ilia Prikhodko∗

iliaprikhodko1888@gmail.com

November 14, 2026


Abstract

This paper presents a novel navigation system for 24-tone equal temperament (24TET), derived from the theory of well-formed scales (Carey & Clampitt, 1989) and maximally even sets (Clough & Douthett, 1991; Krantz & Douthett, 2000). We demonstrate that the units modulo 24, U (24) = {1, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23}, form four self-dual pairs of interval generators: {+1, +23}, {+5, +19}, {+7, +17}, and

{+11, +13}. For the diatonic region (d = 7), the equation dg ≡ ±1 (mod 24) yields two solutions: g = 7 and g = 17. These generators induce four independent unidirec-tional proximity cycles, enabling smooth modulation between two interlocked 12TET subsystems (even and odd pitch classes). We introduce the Harmonic Compass

— a structural framework comprising these four cycles, seven well-formed modes of region R(24, 7), nine triad classes, and six structural anchors (diminished seventh chords). We also introduce a two-level harmonic architecture: (1) navigational scales (well-formed modes for modulation) and (2) functional modes (including a 10-step microchromatic mode S10 = {0, 3, 6, 8, 11, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23} derived from Jędrzejew-ski’s limited transposition sets). This work extends the mathematical theory of mu-sical scales to microtonal temperaments while preserving the perceptual smoothness of diatonic structures.

Keywords: 24TET, well-formed scales, unidirectional cycles, microtonality, har-monic compass, maximally even sets, modulation


  1. Introduction

    Twelve-tone equal temperament (12TET) has dominated Western music for over three centuries. Its structure is elegantly simple: the octave is divided into twelve equal semi-tones, and modulation occurs primarily through the Circle of Fifths — a unidirectional cycle generated by the interval of a perfect fifth (7 semitones).

    However, 24-tone equal temperament (24TET), which divides the octave into twenty-four quarter-tones, offers more than simply “twice as many notes.” This paper demon-strates that 24TET possesses a richer navigational structure: four independent self-dual cycles instead of one.


    ∗Independent Researcher

    The theoretical foundation for this discovery lies in the work of Carey and Clampitt (1989) on well-formed scales and regions, Clough and Douthett (1991) on maximally even sets, and Krantz and Douthett (2000) on P-cycles. These authors established that a scale is well-formed if and only if its chromatic cardinality c and diatonic cardinality d are coprime (i.e., gcd(c, d) = 1).

    For 12TET with diatonic scales (c = 12, d = 7), we have gcd(12, 7) = 1, which explains why the diatonic scale works so well in 12TET. Remarkably, for 24TET with the same diatonic cardinality (c = 24, d = 7), we also have gcd(24, 7) = 1. This mathematical property guarantees that 24TET can support well-formed diatonic scales — but with additional structural features unavailable in 12TET.

    The central contribution of this paper is the Harmonic Compass: a complete navi-gational system for 24TET comprising:

    • Four self-dual unidirectional cycles generated by intervals {+1, +5, +7, +11}

    • Seven navigational scales (well-formed modes of region R(24, 7))

    • Nine triad classes derived from step-interval sequences

    • Six structural anchors (diminished seventh chords) that bridge two interlocked 12TET subsystems

    • A ten-note functional mode S10 = {0, 3, 6, 8, 11, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23} derived from Ję-drzejewski’s classification of limited transposition sets

      This system enables smooth modulation not only within each 12TET subsystem but also between them — a capability absent in standard 12TET.

      Remark 1.1 (Novelty Statement). While the mathematical properties of units modulo 24 are known in microtonal theory, this paper contributes a functional navigation framework analogous to the Circle of Fifths in 12TET. Specifically:

    • In 12TET, the tritone (+6, gcd(6, 12) = 6) generates only a 2-element subgroup — a “dead end” for harmonic navigation.

    • In 24TET, the micro-tritone (+11, gcd(11, 24) = 1) generates the entire group Z24

      — a full 24-note cycle analogous to the quintal circle.

    • The Harmonic Compass reveals three navigational layers in 24TET:

      1. Even quintal cycle (+14): 12 notes, isomorphic to 12TET

      2. Odd quintal cycle (+14 from odd start): 12 notes, the “other” 12TET subsystem

      3. Micro-tritone cycle (+11): 24 notes, bridges both subsystems

    • We introduce the three-point turn: a minimal compositional gesture that switches between these cycles, enabling functional harmonic motion unavailable in 12TET.

    • We propose a two-level harmonic architecture distinguishing navigational scales (well-formed) from functional modes (optimised for composition).

    1. Related Work

      The Harmonic Compass builds upon several established strands of music-theoretical re-search: group-theoretic approaches to equal temperaments, the theory of well-formed scales and maximally even sets, and prior explorations of 24-tone equal temperament (24TET).

      Group-theoretic foundations. Balzano (1980) demonstrated that equal tempera-ments can be analysed as cyclic groups Zc, and that microtonal systems often contain smaller isomorphic subsystems. For 24TET, his framework reveals a subgroup of index 2 (the even pitch classes {0, 2, 4, . . . , 22}) and its coset (the odd pitch classes). This di-

      rectly supports our Theorem 3.7, which shows that odd generators {1, 5, 7, 11} necessarily

      alternate between the two subsystems. Jędrzejewski (2006, 2023) provides a compre-

      hensive mathematical treatment of 24-tone rows and scales, confirming the role of units modulo 24, U (24) = {1, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23}, as the set of invertible intervals that can generate the entire pitch space.

      Well-formed scales and maximally even sets. Carey and Clampitt (1989) estab-lished the theory of well-formed scales, showing that a scale with chromatic cardinality c and diatonic cardinality d is well-formed iff gcd(c, d) = 1 and the generator g satisfies dg ≡ ±1 (mod c). For 24TET with d = 7, this yields the two generators g = 7 and g = 17 that form the diatonic backbone of the Harmonic Compass. Maximally even sets were first formalised by Clough and Douthett (1991), who proved that well-formed scales are a subset of maximally even sets. Krantz and Douthett (2000) later extended this the-ory to P-cycles (proximity cycles), where adjacent sets differ by minimal voice-leading. Our distinction between true P-cycle modulations (generator +7) and generator-based modulations (e.g., +11) follows directly from this taxonomy.

      Prior work on 24TET and microtonal harmony. Blackwood (1991) explored modal and chordal possibilities in several equal temperaments, including 24TET, provid-ing a historical precedent for harmonic approaches beyond 12TET. Žabka (2010) gener-alised Carey and Clampitt’s theorem to two-dimensional well-formedness, discussing the 24TET system in the context of historical microtonal tunings such as the Indian 22-śruti. Flieder (2025) recently addressed the mathematical embedding of smaller pitch spaces (like 12TET) into larger temperaments (like 24TET), offering a contemporary group-theoretic validation of our “interlocked subsystems” view.

      Limited transposition sets. Jędrzejewski (2006, Chapter 3.4) classified 381 limited transposition sets in 24TET using isotropy groups H = kZ24. These sets do not generate all 24 pitch classes under transposition (gcd(g, 24) ̸= 1). Our ten-note functional mode S10 = {0, 3, 6, 8, 11, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23} belongs to this family, specifically the 66 sets of cardinality 10 for k = 12.

      What is new in the Harmonic Compass. While previous work has established the mathematical properties of Z24 and the applicability of well-formed scales to microtonal systems, no prior study has:

      1. Identified the four canonical generators {+1, +5, +7, +11} as a complete navi-gation system for 24TET, explicitly linking each generator to a distinct region (R(24, 1), R(24, 5), R(24, 7), R(24, 11));

      2. Distinguished between true P-cycle modulations (minimal voice-leading) and generator-based modulations (parallel transposition by a unit interval) within a single coherent framework;

      3. Provided a concrete harmonic vocabulary for 24TET comprising seven naviga-tional scales, nine triad classes, and six structural anchors (diminished seventh chords) specifically designed for quarter-tone harmony;

      4. Introduced the concept of unlimited transposition cycles as the complement to Jędrzejewski’s limited transposition sets;

      5. Proposed a two-level harmonic architecture distinguishing navigational scales (well-formed) from functional modes (optimised for composition).

      The Harmonic Compass fills this gap, offering composers and theorists a practical tool for navigation and modulation in 24TET while preserving the mathematical rigour of well-formed scale theory.


  2. Theoretical Background

    1. Well-Formed Scales and Regions

      Carey and Clampitt (1989) defined a well-formed scale as a connected subset of Pythagorean pitch space Pˆ that satisfies specific mathematical conditions. The key insight is that well-formed scales are generated by a single interval (the generator) and consist of exactly two distinct step sizes.

      Definition 2.1 (Well-Formed Scale). A scale with chromatic cardinality c and diatonic cardinality d is well-formed if it can be generated by a single interval g (i.e., all pitches are of the form k·g mod c for k = 0, 1, . . . , d−1) and consists of exactly two distinct step sizes. A necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of such a scale is gcd(c, d) = 1, with the generator g satisfying the linear Diophantine equation:

      dg ≡ ±1 (mod c) (1)

      For the diatonic scale in 12TET (c = 12, d = 7), equation (1) yields g ∈ {5, 7} — the perfect fourth and perfect fifth, which generate the familiar Circle of Fifths. For 24TET with the same diatonic cardinality (c = 24, d = 7), equation (1) yields g ∈ {7, 17}, the two generators that form the diatonic backbone of the Harmonic Compass.


    2. Maximally Even Sets and P-Cycles

      Clough and Douthett (1991) introduced the concept of maximally even (ME) sets, which distribute d elements as evenly as possible around a chromatic circle of c notes. The ME algorithm generates these sets using the formula:


      n

      J(c,d) =

      ck + n

      d


      mod c


      d−1


      k=0


      (2)

      where n ∈ {0, 1, . . . , c − 1} is the index of transposition.

      Krantz and Douthett (2000) extended this theory by defining P-cycles (proximity cy-

      cles) as cycles of sets where adjacent members differ by minimal voice-leading — specifi-cally, where all but one note remain fixed, and the moving note changes by precisely one chromatic step.

      Definition 2.2 (Unidirectional P-Cycle). A P-cycle is unidirectional if the sets in the cy-cle exhaust the entire set class, visiting all c transpositions before returning to the starting point.

      The Circle of Fifths in 12TET is a classic example of a unidirectional P-cycle.

      Definition 2.3 (Unlimited Transposition Cycle). A generator g ∈ Z24 induces an unlim-ited transposition cycle if gcd(g, 24) = 1, i.e., if it generates the entire group Z24 under repeated transposition. The Harmonic Compass consists of the four canonical unlimited transposition cycles {+1, +5, +7, +11}.


    3. Regions and Complementarity

      Carey and Clampitt introduced the concept of regions R(A, B), which are maximal con-nected sets of complements in the group G(A, B). Each region contains a modal system of well-formed scales. The regions are determined by convergents and semi-convergents of the continued fraction expansion of log2 3.

      For our purposes, the diatonic region R(11, 7) in 12TET extends to R(24, 7) in 24TET, preserving the well-formed property while expanding structural possibilities.


  3. The Harmonic Compass: Mathematical Derivation

    1. Solving the Generator Equation for 24TET

      For 24TET with diatonic cardinality d = 7, we solve equation (1):

      7g ≡ ±1 (mod 24) (3)

      Proposition 3.1. The set of interval generators that can induce unidirectional cycles in 24TET is precisely the set of units modulo 24:

      U (24) = {g ∈ Z24 | gcd(g, 24) = 1} = {1, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23}

      Remark 3.2. For the specific case of diatonic scales (d = 7), equation (3) has exactly two solutions:

      g = 7 (7 × 7 = 49 ≡ 1 (mod 24)), g = 17 (7 × 17 = 119 ≡ 23 ≡ −1 (mod 24)).

      These correspond to the fifth and its inversion in the diatonic region R(24, 7). Proof. We verify which elements of U (24) satisfy equation (3):

      7 × 1 = 7 ≢ ±1 (mod 24)

      7 × 5 = 35 ≡ 11 ≢ ±1 (mod 24)

      7 × 7 = 49 ≡ 1 (mod 24) ✓

      7 × 11 = 77 ≡ 5 ≢ ±1 (mod 24)

      7 × 13 = 91 ≡ 19 ≢ ±1 (mod 24)

      7 × 17 = 119 ≡ 23 ≡ −1 (mod 24) ✓

      7 × 19 = 133 ≡ 13 ≢ ±1 (mod 24)

      7 × 23 = 161 ≡ 17 ≢ ±1 (mod 24)

      Thus, for d = 7, only g ∈ {7, 17} are solutions. However, all eight units modulo 24 serve as potential generators for well-formed scales with various diatonic cardinalities d satisfying gcd(d, 24) = 1.

      These eight units form four self-dual pairs:

      {1, 23}, {5, 19}, {7, 17}, {11, 13}

      where each pair consists of an interval and its inversion (since g + g′ = 24).

      Convention 3.3 (Canonical Generator Selection). For each self-dual pair {g, 24 − g}, we select the generator g < 12 as the canonical representative. This convention ensures consistent naming across the Harmonic Compass.


    2. The Four Cycles

      Each generator induces a unidirectional P-cycle. We select the four canonical generators

      {+1, +5, +7, +11} to form the Harmonic Compass:

      1. Cycle +1 (Micro-Chromatic): Step size 50¢. Generates all 24 notes through quarter-tone motion.

      2. Cycle +5 (Half-Fourth): Step size 250¢. This interval is half the size of the perfect fourth (10 steps, 500¢) in 24TET. Perceptually, it may be heard as a “wide major second” or “quarter-fourth” depending on context.

      3. Cycle +7 (Half-Fifth / Neutral Third): Step size 350¢. This interval is half the size of the perfect fifth (14 steps, 700¢) in 24TET. Perceptually, it may be heard as a “short fourth” (Amiot, personal communication, 2026). Structurally, it serves as a bridge between the even and odd 12TET subsystems.

      4. Cycle +11 (Micro-Tritone): Step size 550¢. A microtonal tritone that visits all 24 notes (unlike the 12TET tritone, which cycles between only 2 notes).

        Proposition 3.4. Each of the four cycles is self-dual: traversing the cycle in the forward direction (generator g) or backward direction (generator 24 − g) produces the same set of pitch classes, merely in reverse order.

        Proof. For any generator g ∈ {1, 5, 7, 11}, its complement is g′ = 24 − g. Since g + g′ ≡ 0 (mod 24), applying g repeatedly k times yields the pitch class k · g mod 24, while applying g′ repeatedly k times yields k · (24 − g) ≡ −k · g (mod 24). Thus the backward cycle is exactly the forward cycle traversed in reverse order, visiting the same set of pitch

        classes.

        Remark 3.5 (Interval Naming Conventions in 24TET). The naming of intervals in 24TET depends on the chosen interpretive framework:

        • Global Continuum View: The perfect fifth is +14 steps (700¢), and +7 (350¢) is a “half-fifth.”

        • Dual-System View: Within each 12TET subsystem (even/odd), functional har-mony operates with intervals measured in subsystem steps.

        • Generative View: Independent of perceptual naming, +7 is a unit modulo 24 (gcd(7, 24) = 1) and thus a valid generator for well-formed scales.

      In this paper, we adopt the Generative View for mathematical rigor, while acknowledging the perceptual nuances noted above.

      Remark 3.6 (Scope of the Harmonic Compass). The Harmonic Compass is designed as a navigation system for the entire 24TET space, not solely for a single well-formed region. Of the four canonical generators:

      • +7 canonically generates the well-formed region R(24, 7);

      • +5 canonically generates the well-formed region R(24, 5);

      • +11 canonically generates the well-formed region R(24, 11);

      • +1 canonically generates the well-formed region R(24, 1).

      This multi-regional coverage enables modulation between different scale types, not merely within one region.


    3. Two Interlocked 12TET Systems

      A crucial structural feature of 24TET is that it contains two interlocked 12TET subsys-tems:

      • Even system: Pitch classes {0, 2, 4, . . . , 22}

      • Odd system: Pitch classes {1, 3, 5, . . . , 23}

      Each subsystem is isomorphic to 12TET, shifted by 50 cents relative to the other. The four cycles of the Harmonic Compass enable modulation between these systems, not merely within them.

      Theorem 3.7. The cycles +1, +5, +7, and +11 all alternate between even and odd pitch classes at each step, thereby providing smooth voice-leading pathways between the two 12TET subsystems.

      Proof. Since all four generators are odd numbers, adding any generator g ∈ {1, 5, 7, 11} to an even pitch class yields an odd pitch class, and vice versa. Therefore, each cycle strictly alternates between the two subsystems.

      This property is fundamental to the Harmonic Compass: it transforms what could be two isolated 12TET worlds into a single, integrated 24TET universe.


    4. Why Four Cycles? The Collapse of the Octave-Fifth Analogy

      In 12TET, the circle of fifths (generator g = 7) and the octave (generator g = 12) are, in a deep sense, the same cycle. Mathematically, this is because gcd(12, 7) = 1: the generator 7 is a unit modulo 12, meaning it generates the entire group Z12. The octave (+12 ≡ 0) is the trivial cycle of length 1; traversing the fifth cycle 12 times returns to the starting pitch class, having visited all 12 notes. Thus, in 12TET there is essentially one non-trivial complete cycle.

      In 24TET, the situation is fundamentally different. The perfect fifth as an interval of 700¢ corresponds to +14 steps modulo 24. Since gcd(24, 14) = 2 ̸= 1, the generator +14 does not generate the entire group. Instead, it generates only one of the two interlocked 12TET subsystems (even or odd pitch classes, depending on the starting point).

      What, then, is the analogue of the 12TET fifth–octave relationship in 24TET? The true analogues are the units modulo 24 — the eight elements of U (24) = {1, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23}. Each unit with gcd(g, 24) = 1 generates the entire group Z24. Consequently, each such generator produces a full 24-note cycle, visiting every pitch class exactly once before returning to the octave after 24 steps.

      Crucially, the units modulo 24 form four self-dual pairs {g, 24 − g}, each pair rep-resenting the same cycle traversed in opposite directions. This yields four distinct non-trivial complete cycles in 24TET, corresponding to the four canonical generators

      {+1, +5, +7, +11} of the Harmonic Compass:


      Generator

      Step size

      What it “unfolds”

      +1

      50¢

      Chromatic quarter-tone scale

      +5

      250¢

      Half-fourth / quarter-fourth

      +7

      350¢

      Half-fifth / neutral third

      +11

      550¢

      Microtonal tritone

      Each of these four generators unfolds the octave differently, passing through a distinct ordering of the 24 pitch classes. In 12TET, the octave had only one non-trivial unfolding (the fifth). In 24TET, the octave has four — and these four are precisely the cycles of the Harmonic Compass.

      This multiplicity has direct consequences for functional harmony. In 12TET, harmonic function is anchored to the single fifth cycle. In 24TET, there are four independent cycles, and smooth modulation — especially between the even and odd 12TET subsystems — often requires switching from one cycle to another. The three-point turn described in Section 4.4 is one such technique: it moves from the +14 cycle (which generates only a 12TET subsystem) to a generator-based modulation using +1, +5, +7, or +11, thereby crossing between subsystems and creating functional tension that resolves upon returning to the original cycle at a different transposition level.


    5. The Micro-Tritone Cycle: A Full Generator of Z24

      In 12TET, the tritone (+6 steps, 600¢) generates only a 2-element subgroup {0, 6}, since gcd(6, 12) = 6 ̸= 1. This is a structural “dead end” — no harmonic navigation system analogous to the Circle of Fifths can be built from the tritone in 12TET.

      In 24TET, the situation is fundamentally different. The micro-tritone (+11 steps, 550¢) satisfies gcd(11, 24) = 1, and therefore generates the entire group Z24:


      0 → 11 → 22 → 9 → 20 → 7 → 18 → 5 → 16 → 3 → 14 → 1 →

      12 → 23 → 10 → 21 → 8 → 19 → 6 → 17 → 4 → 15 → 2 → 13 → 0

      This 24-note cycle is structurally analogous to the Circle of Fifths in 12TET, but with a crucial difference: it intersects both the even and odd quintal cycles (+14), providing a pathway for modulation between the two interlocked 12TET subsystems.

      Remark 3.8 (Three Cycles, Three Functions). The Harmonic Compass thus reveals three distinct navigational layers in 24TET:

      • Even quintal cycle (+14): intra-system modulation within the even 12TET sub-system

      • Odd quintal cycle (+14 from odd start): intra-system modulation within the odd 12TET subsystem

      • Micro-tritone cycle (+11): inter-system modulation between the two subsystems

      Functional harmony in 24TET can be understood as controlled switching between these three cycles.


    6. Fundamental Harmonic Domain

      The ten-note functional mode constructed in Section 4.5,

      S10 = {0, 3, 6, 8, 11, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23},

      can be understood as a fundamental harmonic domain for 24TET. Under repeated trans-position by the micro-tritone generator +11, S10 generates 24 distinct transpositions be-fore returning to the original set, thereby exhaustively covering the pitch-class space Z24.

      Remark 3.9 (Analogy with Geometric Topology). This structure is conceptually analo-gous to a fundamental domain in geometric topology, where a subset of a space — together with the action of a symmetry group — tiles the entire space. Here, S10 plays the role of the domain, and the cyclic group generated by T11 (transposition by +11) acts as the symmetry group. The fact that S10 contains 10 out of 24 pitch classes and that T11 cy-cles through all 24 distinct transpositions demonstrates that S10 is an optimal harmonic “cutout” that reveals the global structure of Z24.

      This analogy is structural rather than formal: we do not claim mathematical equiv-alence with topological fundamental domains, but rather highlight the shared principle of finding an invariant subset whose transformations under a group action exhaust the parent space.

      This perspective connects the Harmonic Compass to deeper principles in mathemat-ics, where identifying invariant subsets under group actions often leads to a complete understanding of the space itself.


    7. Relation to Jędrzejewski’s Limited Transposition Sets

      Jędrzejewski (2006, 2023) classified 381 limited transposition sets in 24TET using isotropy groups H = kZ24 where k ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12}. These are sets that do not generate all 24 pitch classes under transposition (gcd(g, 24) ̸= 1).

      The Harmonic Compass operates on the complementary principle: the four canonical generators {+1, +5, +7, +11} satisfy gcd(g, 24) = 1, meaning they generate the entire group Z24. We propose the term unlimited transposition cycles for this class.

      Remark 3.10 (Two Complementary Classes). 24TET pitch structures can be divided into two complementary classes:

      • Unlimited transposition cycles (Harmonic Compass): 4 generators with gcd(g, 24) = 1, producing full 24-note cycles for navigation and modulation.

      • Limited transposition sets (Jędrzejewski): 381 sets with gcd(g, 24) ̸= 1, used for harmonic coloration and functional modes.

      The ten-note functional mode S10 = {0, 3, 6, 8, 11, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23} falls into Jędrzejew-ski’s category k = 12, one of 66 sets of 10 notes (Jędrzejewski 2006, Chapter 3.4, p. 75). This confirms its status as a functional mode rather than a navigational cycle.


    8. All Well-Formed Scales Modulo 24

      The units modulo 24, U (24) = {1, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23}, serve as potential generators for well-formed scales with various diatonic cardinalities d satisfying gcd(d, 24) = 1.

      Table 1 lists all non-reducible well-formed scales in 24TET, their generators, and musical interpretations. This table demonstrates that the four canonical generators

      {+1, +5, +7, +11} selected for the Harmonic Compass correspond to the four fundamen-tal regions: trivial (d = 1), pentatonic (d = 5), diatonic (d = 7), and chromatic (d = 11). Each generator pair {g, 24 − g} produces complementary well-formed scales, reflecting the self-dual structure of the system.

  4. Musical Implications

    1. Seven Navigational Scales (Well-Formed Modes of Region R(24,7))

      Applying the ME algorithm (2) with c = 24 and d = 7 yields seven distinct modes. These are the navigational scales of the Harmonic Compass — well-formed structures used for modulation and cycle switching. Each mode consists of two step sizes: 3 steps (150¢) and 4 steps (200¢), arranged in different patterns.

      1. Derivation of the Seven Navigational Scales from Generator +7

        Starting from pitch class 0 and applying generator g = 7 repeatedly modulo 24:


        Step 0:

        0

        Step 1:

        0 + 7 = 7

        Step 2:

        7 + 7 = 14

        Step 3:

        14 + 7 = 21

        Step 4:

        21 + 7 = 28 ≡ 4 (mod 24)

        Step 5:

        4 + 7 = 11

        Step 6:

        11 + 7 = 18

        This yields the scale {0, 7, 14, 21, 4, 11, 18}, which when sorted becomes: {0, 4, 7, 11, 14, 18, 21}

        — identical to Mode 1.

        The remaining six modes are cyclic rotations of this scale, starting from each of the seven pitch classes.

        The seven navigational scales are:


        Mode 1:

        {0, 4, 7, 11, 14, 18, 21}

        Mode 2:

        {1, 4, 7, 11, 14, 18, 21}

        Mode 3:

        {1, 4, 8, 11, 14, 18, 21}

        Mode 4:

        {1, 4, 8, 11, 15, 18, 21}

        Mode 5:

        {1, 4, 8, 11, 15, 18, 22}

        Mode 6:

        {1, 5, 8, 11, 15, 18, 22}

        Mode 7:

        {1, 5, 8, 12, 15, 18, 22}

        These navigational scales preserve the perceptual “smoothness” of diatonic scales while offering microtonal coloration unavailable in 12TET. Their well-formed structure (gcd(24, 7) = 1) makes them ideal for systematic modulation via the four cycles of the Harmonic Compass.


    2. Nine Triad Classes

      Following Krantz and Douthett’s method of deriving triads from step-interval sequences, we identify nine distinct triad classes in 24TET:

      1. Minor triad: {0, 6, 14} — intervals (300¢, 400¢)

      2. Major triad: {0, 8, 14} — intervals (400¢, 300¢)

      3. M-Chord: {0, 7, 14} — intervals (350¢, 350¢) — symmetric, proposed as potential tonal center

      4. Micro-minor variants: {0, 6, 13}, {0, 7, 13}

      5. Micro-major variants: {0, 7, 15}, {0, 8, 15}

      6. Tritone-based: {0, 5, 13}, {0, 8, 13}

      The M-Chord {0, 7, 14} is particularly significant: its symmetry (two equal intervals of 350¢) distinguishes it from traditional major/minor triads. However, as Sethares (2005) notes, intervals near 350¢ can exhibit high sensory dissonance depending on timbre. Fur-ther empirical research is therefore needed to establish its perceptual stability as a tonal center in musical contexts.


    3. Six Structural Anchors

      The six diminished seventh chords in 24TET serve as structural anchors — harmonic nodes that bridge the even and odd 12TET systems:


      Anchor 1:

      {0, 6, 12, 18}

      Anchor 2:

      {1, 7, 13, 19}

      Anchor 3:

      {2, 8, 14, 20}

      Anchor 4:

      {3, 9, 15, 21}

      Anchor 5:

      {4, 10, 16, 22}

      Anchor 6:

      {5, 11, 17, 23}

      Each anchor contains two notes from the even system and two from the odd system, making it an ideal pivot chord for modulation between the two 12TET subsystems.


    4. Modulation via Cycle Switching

      The Harmonic Compass enables modulation through two distinct mechanisms:

      1. P-Cycle Modulation (intra-system): Moving by cycle +7 within a single 12TET subsystem produces minimal voice-leading, analogous to traditional modulation in 12TET:

        {0, 8, 14} → {7, 15, 21} (one note moves by 50¢)

      2. Generator-Based Modulation (inter-system): Moving by cycle +11 or +13 switches between the even and odd subsystems. We term the minimal gesture that ac-complishes this a three-point turn:

        1. Begin in the even quintal cycle (e.g., {0, 8, 14})

        2. Step by +11 or +13 — enter the micro-tritone cycle

        3. Step again — return to the even (or odd) quintal cycle, but on a different scale degree

          Remark 4.1 (Three-Point Turn). The three-point turn is to 24TET what the dominant-tonic cadence is to 12TET: a minimal harmonic gesture that creates functional tension and resolution through cycle switching rather than mere position-shifting within a single cycle.

      3. Quartal Modulation: Moving by cycle +5 offers an alternative pathway with distinct harmonic color.

      In each case, the voice-leading is context-dependent: cycle +7 provides minimal voice-leading within a subsystem, while cycles +5 and +11 offer inter-system modulation with richer harmonic displacement.

    5. Functional Modes vs. Navigational Scales

      The Harmonic Compass distinguishes two complementary levels of harmonic organization in 24TET:


      Table 2: Two Levels of Harmonic Organization in 24TET

      Aspect

      Navigational Scales

      Functional Modes

      Purpose

      Modulation, cycle switching

      Composition, cadences, melody

      Mathematical status

      Well-formed (gcd(c, d) = 1)

      Not required (gcd(c, d) ̸= 1 OK)

      Example

      7 modes of R(24, 7) (Section 4.1)

      10-step microchromatic mode S10

      Analogy in 12TET

      Chromatic scale (generative)

      Diatonic scale (functional)

      Generator

      Single interval (g = 7 or g = 17)

      Composite (multiple intervals)


      Navigational Scales are mathematically well-formed scales derived from the units modulo 24 (Section 3.8). For the diatonic region R(24, 7), these comprise the seven modes generated by g = 7 or g = 17 (Section 4.1). They provide the structural backbone for modulation via the four canonical cycles of the Harmonic Compass.

      Functional Modes are scale structures optimised for compositional use, includ-ing tonal cadences and voice-leading coherence. They need not satisfy the strict well-formedness condition gcd(c, d) = 1. One example is the following 10-step microchromatic mode:

      S10 = {0, 3, 6, 8, 11, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23} (4)

      Its step-interval pattern (in quarter-tone steps) is:

      [3, 3, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 2, 3, 1] (sum = 24)


      1. Why 10 Steps?

        The choice of 10 notes arises from empirical exploration. Patterns with 10 notes produced the smoothest ascending and descending streams when realised as major triads in Ableton, comparable to the diatonic scale’s smooth progression in 12TET. Patterns with 9 or 11 notes exhibited irregular voice-leading.

        This aligns with Jędrzejewski’s enumeration of 66 ten-note limited transposition sets (Jędrzejewski 2006, Chapter 3.4), suggesting that 10 is a mathematically privileged car-dinality for functional modes in 24TET.


      2. Mathematical Status

        Although gcd(24, 10) = 2 ̸= 1, so S10 is not well-formed in the strict sense of Carey & Clampitt (1989), it exhibits:

        • Near-maximal evenness: ideal spacing for 10 notes in 24TET is 2.4 steps; S10

          uses only steps of size 1, 2, or 3 (Clough & Douthett, 1991)

        • Leading-tone function: the final step (23 → 0 = 50) creates tonal resolution analogous to the leading tone in 12TET

        • Wave-like symmetry: ascending and descending sequences form complementary streams when realised as chord progressions

      3. Cyclic Progression Matrix

        The ten-note mode S10 generates a cyclic progression that visits each of its elements exactly once when realised as a sequence of major triads:

        0, 8, 18, 6, 20, 23, 15, 3, 11, 13

        Extending this progression by the same interval pattern yields a closed cycle of 18 steps:

        0, 8, 18, 6, 20, 23, 15, 3, 11, 13, 21, 7, 19, 9, 12, 4, 16, 0

        Transposing this cycle by +2 generates a 12×18 matrix (see supplementary materials), where each row corresponds to a distinct tonal centre (all even pitch classes). This ma-trix provides a rich resource for compositional exploration, offering multiple progression lengths and systematic modulation paths.

        Remark 4.2 (Two-Level Harmony in 24TET). Just as 12TET distinguishes the diatonic scale (functional) from the chromatic scale (generative), 24TET can distinguish functional modes (e.g., S10) from navigational scales (well-formed modes of R(24, 7)). The Harmonic Compass provides pathways for modulation between functional modes via the navigational cycles. For example, a three-point turn (Section 4.4) can switch the tonal center of the ten-note mode from one pitch class to another, enabling harmonic motion that retains the mode’s characteristic interval pattern.


  5. Discussion

    1. Comparison with Other Temperaments

      The 24TET system occupies a unique position among equal temperaments:

      • 12TET: One Circle of Fifths, limited modulation paths

      • 24TET: Four independent cycles, rich modulation possibilities

      • 31TET: Better approximation of just intervals, but more complex

      • 53TET: Excellent approximation, but impractical for performance

      24TET offers a “sweet spot”: it doubles the resolution of 12TET while remaining performable on existing instruments (with retuning) and preserving the familiar diatonic structure.


    2. Historical Context

      Quarter-tone music has been explored since the early 20th century by composers such as Alois Hába, Ivan Wyschnegradsky, and Harry Partch. These pioneers developed both melodic and harmonic resources for microtonal music. Hába’s Neue Harmonielehre des diatonischen, chromatischen, Viertel-, Drittel-, Sechstel- und Zwölfteltonsystems (1927) systematically addresses chordal structures and voice-leading not only in quarter-tones but also in finer divisions (third-, sixth-, and twelfth-tones). Wyschnegradsky’s writings on quarter-tone harmony similarly explore harmonic possibilities.

      However, a systematic framework for harmonic navigation in 24TET — including explicit modulation pathways between interlocked 12TET subsystems, a taxonomy of triad classes derived from maximally even sets, structural anchors for pivot chords, and a two-level architecture distinguishing navigational scales from functional modes — has not been previously formalised. The Harmonic Compass provides such a framework, extending the theoretical foundations laid by these pioneers while introducing new concepts (P-cycle vs. generator-based modulation, the four canonical cycles, unlimited transposition cycles) that are unique to the 24TET space.1


    3. Limitations and Future Directions

      Several limitations warrant acknowledgment:

      1. Perceptual learning: Listeners accustomed to 12TET may require exposure to internalize the harmonic functions of 24TET.

      2. Instrumental constraints: Most Western instruments are designed for 12TET. While retuning is possible, it requires specialized equipment or software.

      3. Notational challenges: Standard notation is inadequate for 24TET. Alternative notations (e.g., numbers, quarter-tone accidentals) require further standardization.

        Future research directions include:

        • Empirical studies of listener perception of 24TET harmony

        • Development of instrumental techniques and pedagogical methods

        • Exploration of other well-formed regions (e.g., R(24, 5) and R(24, 11))

        • Computational tools for composition and analysis in 24TET

        • Further investigation of the 66 ten-note limited transposition sets (Jędrzejewski 2006) for potential additional functional modes

        • Systematic comparison of the ten-note mode with traditional microtonal scales (e.g., Arabic maqamat, Indian shrutis)


  6. Conclusion

This paper has presented the Harmonic Compass — a comprehensive navigational sys-tem for 24-tone equal temperament. By extending the theoretical frameworks of Carey and Clampitt (1989), Clough and Douthett (1991), Krantz and Douthett (2000), and Jędrzejewski (2006), we have demonstrated that:

  1. The units modulo 24, U (24) = {1, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23}, form four self-dual pairs of generators. For the diatonic region (d = 7), the equation dg ≡ ±1 (mod 24) has exactly two solutions: g = 7 and g = 17.


    1The Harmonic Compass extends Hába’s harmonic foundation by introducing the four canonical gener-

    ators {1, 5, 7, 11} as a complete navigation system and the distinction between P-cycle and generator-based modulation.

  2. The micro-tritone (+11, 550¢) generates the entire group Z24, unlike the tritone in 12TET (+6, 600¢), which generates only a 2-element subgroup. This enables a full 24-note navigation cycle analogous to the Circle of Fifths in 12TET.

  3. 24TET contains three navigational layers: even quintal (+14), odd quintal (+14 from odd start), and micro-tritone (+11). The Harmonic Compass provides explicit pathways for modulation within and between these layers.

  4. We introduce the three-point turn: a minimal compositional gesture that switches between cycles, creating functional harmonic motion unavailable in 12TET.

  5. We propose a two-level harmonic architecture distinguishing navigational scales (well-formed modes for modulation) from functional modes (optimised for composition). The system comprises seven navigational scales, nine triad classes, six structural anchors, and a ten-note functional mode S10 = {0, 3, 6, 8, 11, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23}.

  6. We distinguish between unlimited transposition cycles (Harmonic Compass, gcd(g, 24) = 1) and limited transposition sets (Jędrzejewski, gcd(g, 24) ̸= 1), clarifying the complementary roles of navigational and functional structures in 24TET.

    The Harmonic Compass is not merely a mathematical curiosity; it is a functional nav-igation framework for 24TET, analogous to the Circle of Fifths in 12TET but with richer structural possibilities. Its two-level architecture — navigational scales for modulation, functional modes for composition — provides composers, theorists, and performers a sys-tematic tool for harmonic exploration beyond 12TET while retaining structural rigor and perceptual smoothness.

    As microtonal music continues to gain traction in the 21st century, systems like the Harmonic Compass offer a bridge between the familiar and the novel — between the mathematical elegance of well-formed scales and the creative possibilities of quarter-tone harmony.

    The Harmonic Sphere of 24TET: Universal Navigation, Cycle Anchors, and Tonal

    Breathing

    Ilia Prikhodko∗

    iliaprikhodko1888@gmail.com

    November 14, 2026


    Abstract

    This paper constructs a complete structural and compositional system for 24-tone equal temperament (24TET) centred on a 10-note structural mode (generative set) S10 = {0, 3, 6, 8, 11, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23}. We demonstrate that S10 functions as a universal navigator : it contains all eight units of U (24) as internal intervals, making it capable of accessing every pitch class and every canonical generator from within its own structure. Its step-interval pattern harbours three invariant palindromes—its mode signature—present in all 24 transpositions. We define a proximity metric d(k) = |S10 ∩ (S10 + k)|, prove its symmetry, and show that the tritone transposition (k = 12, 600¢) shares 8 of 10 notes with the tonic—mathematically the second-highest overlap after the identity (whether this translates to perceptual closeness is an empirical question). This pair of poles forms a unique tonal breath: the tonic pole’s two unique notes span an interval of 13 quarter-tone steps (650¢, inhalation), while the tritone pole’s span 11 (550¢, exhalation). We introduce the Tritone Flip, a minimal compositional gesture shifting only two voices by 50¢ each while eight remain fixed. Reinterpreting six microtonally altered diminished seventh chords not as vertical sonorities but as cycle anchors built from alternating +5 and +7 gen-erators, we show that they form a bridge network —a system of symmetry bridges connecting all 24 transpositions of S10 into a coherent graph. We then develop a taxonomy of compositional trajectories through this space, demonstrating how the graph’s structural features translate into concrete harmonic progressions. A set-specific selection principle is identified: of twelve theoretically possible alternating

    +5/+7 cycles in Z24, exactly half are activated by S10 as cycle anchors; the re-maining six persist as silent cycles—geometrically valid but harmonically inert with respect to S10. The resulting Harmonic Sphere—a 48-state space parameterised by transposition and mode—provides composers with a systematic framework for microtonal tonality grounded in structural invariance, spectral resonance, and the breath-like motion between tonic and tritone poles.

    Keywords: 24TET, harmonic sphere, microtonal tonality, universal navigator, cycle anchors, mode signature, tonal breathing, Tritone Flip, compositional space, set-specific selection, silent cycles

    1. Introduction

      Twelve-tone equal temperament (12TET) organises tonal space around the Circle of Fifths, a perfect fifth (+7 semitones, 700¢). This cycle visits all 12 pitch classes be-fore returning, and the entire edifice of Western functional harmony—dominant-tonic relations, diatonic scales, chromatic modulation—rests upon it.

      Twenty-four-tone equal temperament (24TET) divides the octave into 24 quarter-tone steps of 50¢ each, more than doubling available pitch material. Its mathematical structure admits four independent generative cycles. In prior work, we identified these as the four self-dual pairs of units modulo 24: {+1, +23}, {+5, +19}, {+7, +17}, and

      {+11, +13} (Prikhodko, 2026). Each generator produces a complete 24-note cycle, al-ternating between the two interlocked 12TET subsystems—even {0, 2, 4, . . . , 22} and odd

      {1, 3, 5, . . . , 23}—at every step.

      The present paper moves from navigation—identifying these cycles—to tonality : con-

      structing a complete structural harmonic system for 24TET. At its centre is a 10-note structural mode, S10, which we demonstrate to be a universal navigator : its interval structure contains all eight canonical generators, enabling access to the entire 24TET space from any of its transpositions. Its step pattern possesses a mode signature—three nested palindromes invariant under all 24 transpositions. Its proximity structure reveals the tritone (k = 12) as mathematically the second-closest transposition after the tonic, inverting 12TET intuition (whether this mathematical closeness translates to perception is an empirical question). The two poles form a tonal breath: a contraction from an inter-val of 13 quarter-tone steps (inhalation) to one of 11 (exhalation), moving only two voices by a single quarter-tone each.

      We reinterpret six microtonally altered diminished seventh chords as cycle anchors—cyclic trajectories built from alternating +5 and +7 steps. These anchors form a bridge network connecting all 24 transpositions of S10 into a single structural graph. From this graph we derive a systematic taxonomy of compositional trajectories, turning struc-tural invariants into actionable harmonic progressions. A set-specific selection principle is identified: of twelve theoretically possible alternating +5/+7 cycles in Z24, exactly half are activated by S10; the remaining six persist as silent cycles—geometrically valid but harmonically inert. The resulting Harmonic Sphere—a 48-state space parameterised by transposition k ∈ Z24 and mode m ∈ {0, 1}—provides a complete topological and compositional model for microtonal tonality.

    2. S10: Universal Navigator of 24TET

      1. Definition and Structure

        Definition 2.1 (Structural Mode S10). The ten-note structural mode (generative set) in 24TET is defined as:

        S10 = {0, 3, 6, 8, 11, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23} ⊂ Z24. (1)

        The mode contains five even pitch classes {0, 6, 8, 18, 20} and five odd pitch classes

        {3, 11, 13, 15, 23}. Its step-interval pattern (in quarter-tone steps) is:

        [3, 3, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 2, 3, 1] (sum = 24). (2)

        This pattern uses only steps of sizes 1, 2, and 3 quarter-tones, giving the mode near-maximal evenness for 10 notes in 24TET (ideal spacing 2.4 steps). The final step (23 → 0 = 50¢) is a quarter-tone step. In any equal temperament, the pitch class one step below the octave may create a leading-tone analogue; whether this reduced step size (50¢) produces a perceptually distinct cadential effect analogous to the 100¢ semitone resolution in 12TET requires empirical investigation (see Section 11.11).

        S10 belongs to Jędrzejewski’s (2006) classification of limited transposition sets (one of 66 sets of cardinality 10 with isotropy group H = 12Z24). It is not well-formed in the strict sense (gcd(24, 10) = 2 ̸= 1; Carey & Clampitt, 1989), but its near-maximal evenness (Clough & Douthett, 1991) and internal interval structure give it functional properties that exceed those of any well-formed scale in 24TET.


      2. S10 Contains All Eight Canonical Generators

        The units modulo 24, U (24) = {1, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23}, are precisely the intervals that generate complete 24-note cycles. A universal navigator in 24TET would be a set of pitch classes that contains every unit of U (24) as an interval between some pair of its members.

        Proposition 2.1 (Universal Navigation Property). Every transposition S10(k) for k ∈ Z24

        contains all eight units of U (24) as intervals between its notes.

        Proof. Direct computation. For S10(0), the complete interval vector between all pairs of notes includes all eight units. Table 2 lists representative occurrences for each generator. Intervals are measured in the additive group Z24. Since transposition preserves interval structure, the property holds for all S10(k).

        This property distinguishes S10 from any well-formed scale in 24TET. A 7-note diatonic scale in 24TET (generated by +7 or +17) contains only a subset of U (24) as internal intervals. S10, despite being larger, achieves complete navigational capacity: from any note in the mode, every other note in 24TET can be reached via a canonical generator without leaving the mode’s pitch material.


      3. Mode Signature: Palindromic Invariants

        The step-interval pattern of S10 exhibits a deeper structural invariance. When examined cyclically, it contains three nested palindromic subsequences that persist across all 24 transpositions. We term this the mode signature of S10—analogous to a key signature in 12TET, but governing internal structure rather than pitch content.

        Proposition 2.2 (Mode Signature). For every transposition S10(k), the cyclic step pat-tern contains:

        1. An 8-step palindrome: [3, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 2, 3]

        2. A 6-step palindrome: [2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 2]

        3. A 4-step palindrome: [3, 2, 2, 3]

          Transposition shifts the position of these palindromes within the cyclic pattern but does not alter their structure.

          Proof. For S10(0) with step pattern [3, 3, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 2, 3, 1], the 8-step palindrome begins

          at position 1 (the second interval): [3, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 2, 3] is its own reverse. The 6-step

          palindrome [2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 2] begins at position 2. The 4-step palindrome [3, 2, 2, 3] begins at position 3. For any S10(k), the step pattern is a cyclic rotation of the original; the same palindromes appear at correspondingly rotated positions. Computational verifica-tion across all 24 transpositions confirms the result.

          The mode signature is the structural basis for the symmetry bridges explored in Section


    1. Spectral Foundation

      The choice of 0 as the tonic of S10 is motivated by acoustic principles. Each of the eight canonical generators of U (24)—the intervals that generate complete 24-note cycles—admits a rational approximation by small integer ratios. Table 3 lists these approximations together with their errors in cents.

      The alignment of S10 with small-integer ratios finds indirect support in neurodynamic models of auditory processing. Large et al. (2016) demonstrated that mode-locking in coupled neural oscillators predicts perceptual stability for intervals approximating simple rational ratios, even when those ratios are not mathematically exact. This suggests a physiological basis for the stability of intervals such as 11/8 (551.3¢, approximated by step 11 at 550¢) and 12/11 (150.6¢, approximated by step 3 at 150¢)—intervals that anchor the spectral and step structure of S10.

      The errors range from 1.32¢ (for +11 and +13) to 4.96¢ (for +1 and +23). The generators +11, +13, +17, and +19 have errors below 3¢. The generators +5 and +7 are within 2.6¢. The extreme generators +1 and +23 have errors near 5¢, which is still acceptable for spectral colouration in 24TET.

      Three structural features ground the mode more deeply in the physics of sound.

      1. The quarter-tone leading-tone analogue. The step 23 → 0 is a single quarter-tone (50¢), the smallest possible interval in 24TET. Note 23 sits at 1150¢, one minimal step below the octave (1200¢). In any equal temperament, the pitch class one step below the octave may function as a leading-tone analogue, being the closest note to the fundamental without being the fundamental. The rational approximation 31/16 (1145¢) places this note in the region of the 31st harmonic—a high but acoustically meaningful partial. In 24TET, this step is half the size of the familiar semitone cadence of 12TET, giving it

        a distinctive micro-gravitational character. Whether this reduced step size produces a perceptually distinct cadential effect requires empirical investigation (see Section 11.11).

      2. The micro-tritone as an overtone anchor. The generator +11 (550¢) corre-sponds to the ratio 11/8 (551.3¢) with an error of 1.32¢. This is the first prime harmonic absent from 12TET, and 24TET provides the best available approximation to it in any equal temperament below 31TET. All ten notes of S10 lie on the +11 cycle (Section 2.3), meaning that the entire mode can be generated by repeated application of this overtone-derived interval. The mode is thus a spectral selection: a subset of the +11 cycle chosen to maximise near-evenness while preserving the acoustic anchor of the 11th overtone.

      3. The 150¢ step. The step pattern of S10 uses only two sizes: 2 quarter-tones (100¢) and 3 quarter-tones (150¢). The 150¢ step corresponds to the ratio 12/11 (150.6¢, error 0.64¢)—the simplest rational approximation available for this interval. This links the internal structure of S10 to the 11th and 12th harmonics, the region of the overtone series that 24TET is uniquely equipped to represent among equal temperaments below 31TET.

      These three features—the quarter-tone leading-tone analogue, the overtone-derived generator, and the 150¢ step—together ground S10 in acoustic reality. The mode’s coher-ence derives from its structural position within the 24TET grid: it is a near-maximally even selection from the +11 cycle whose internal step structure is built from acoustically meaningful intervals.

      As noted by Sethares (2005), spectral fusion depends on timbre: the proposed align-ment is optimal for inharmonic or spectrally matched synthesis, while acoustic instruments may require empirical adjustment of the mode’s tuning or orchestration.


    2. Embedding in the Micro-Tritone Cycle

      Proposition 2.3. All 10 notes of S10 appear in the micro-tritone cycle (+11) at positions:

      [0, 1, 4, 6, 9, 13, 16, 18, 21, 23]. (3)

      Proof. The micro-tritone cycle is:

      0 → 11 → 22 → 9 → 20 → 7 → 18 → 5 → 16 → 3 → 14 → 1 →

      12 → 23 → 10 → 21 → 8 → 19 → 6 → 17 → 4 → 15 → 2 → 13 → 0.

      Checking each note of S10 against this sequence yields the positions above.

      Remark 2.1 (Interval Signature). The interval signature between consecutive notes of S10

      within the +11 cycle is:

      [1, 3, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 3, 2, 1]. (4)

      This sequence is not a strict palindrome—the forward and reverse orders differ outside the central region. However, it exhibits partial symmetry around the central peak (4), with matching subsequences [3, 2, 3] on both sides. The sequence begins and ends with the smallest interval (1), indicating smooth closure of the cycle, while the largest interval

      (4) appears at the centre, contributing to the mode’s distinctive character.


  1. The Proximity Metric

    1. Definition

      To quantify the structural closeness between different transpositions of S10, we introduce a simple combinatorial measure.

      Definition 3.1 (Proximity Metric). The proximity between S10 and its transposition

      S10 + k is:

      d(k) = |S10 ∩ (S10 + k)|, (5)

      where S10 + k = {(x + k) mod 24 | x ∈ S10}.

      This counts the number of pitch classes shared between the original mode and its

      k-step transposition.


    2. Symmetry Theorem

      Theorem 3.1 (Symmetry of Proximity). For all k ∈ Z24:

      d(k) = d(24 − k). (6)

      Proof. x ∈ S10 ∩ (S10 + k) ⇐⇒ x ∈ S10 and x − k ∈ S10. Let y = x − k. Then y ∈ S10∩(S10−k), establishing a bijection between the two intersections. Since −k ≡ 24−k (mod 24), we have d(k) = d(24 − k).


    3. The Proximity Landscape

      Computing d(k) for all 24 transpositions yields a structured landscape of structural close-ness (Figure 1).

      The most striking result is that transposition by k = 12 (the tritone, 600¢) shares 8 of 10 notes with the tonic—mathematically the second-highest overlap after the identity itself. In 12TET, the tritone is the most distant interval; in 24TET with S10, this math-ematical relationship inverts. The tritone’s proximity is a structural consequence of the

      involution x '→ x + 12, which swaps the even and odd subsystems while preserving 80% of the mode’s content.



      Figure 1: The Proximity Wheel: d(k) = |S10(0) ∩ S10(k)| for all 24 transpositions k ∈ Z24. Bar height indicates the number of common pitch classes (maximum 10 at k = 0). The tritone transposition k = 12 (dark bar) shares d(12) = 8 common tones—mathematically the second-highest value after the tonic itself. Generators +5 and +7 (medium gray bars) yield d = 6. The complete symmetry d(k) = d(24 − k) is visible.


      It is important to note that mathematical proximity as defined by d(k) quantifies struc-tural overlap, not perceptual closeness. Whether listeners experience S10(12) as genuinely “close” to S10(0)—or whether they perceive it as distant due to the tritone’s acoustic instability (it has no simple integer-ratio approximation)—is an empirical question that requires systematic perceptual testing.


  2. The Two Poles: Tonic and Tritone

    1. Uniqueness of the Tritone Pole

      Among all 24 transpositions of S10, the tritone pole k = 12 is structurally unique. Table 4 lists the number of pitch classes that are unique to each transposition—notes belonging to S10(k) but not to S10(0).

      Only k = 12 yields exactly two unique notes. All other transpositions (except the identity) replace four or more notes. The tritone pole is thus the minimal perturbation of the tonic—the smallest possible alteration that produces a distinct structural centre. Whether this structural minimality corresponds to perceptual closeness is an empirical question.
