    5. Observations from the Data

      From Table 5, we can make the following empirical observations:

      1. Periodicity. The behavior repeats every 24 steps. The synchronization pattern at start 0 is identical to that at start 24 and start 48.

      2. Two regimes. We define a synchronization regime as a measure of the density of intersection points over a fixed interval (700 quarter-tones). Empirically, two regimes are observed:

        • Slow regime (50 points): occurs when the phase difference between the pat-terns is not a multiple of 4 (modulo 12). The distance between synchronization points alternates as +9 and +19 steps.

        • Fast regime (75–76 points): occurs when the phase difference is a multiple of 4 (modulo 12). The distance between synchronization points alternates as

          +9 and +10 steps.

          The difference in density (50 versus 75) is explained by the fact that in the fast regime, the patterns “slip past” each other with a smaller step, leading to more frequent coincidences.

      3. Fast regime condition. The fast regime occurs only when the starting position of the second pattern is shifted by +4 or +10 relative to the base starting position

        (14). All other shifts produce the slow regime.

      4. 12-note cycles. In every synchronization, the shared notes form a 12-note cycle. This cycle always consists of two groups of 6 notes, each separated by a constant step of +4, with the two groups separated by +9.

      5. Anchor stability. The two groups of 6 notes that make up the 12-note cycle are the same across multiple starting positions — they simply shift and swap.


    6. The Chromatic Filter and the Closed Cycle

      Empirical data reveal that synchronization with the base level (the chromatic pattern 111111) is not universal. The chromatic sequence is highly selective: it synchronizes only with patterns whose base steps form a specific cycle.

      Let us list the base steps of the patterns that successfully synchronize with the chro-matic pattern:

      3, 11, 15, 23 (4)

      These four numbers are not arbitrary. Their structure reveals three fundamental symmetries:

      1. Tritone symmetry. The pair (3, 15) differs by exactly 12 steps (a tritone). The pair (11, 23) also differs by 12.

      2. Symmetry under the involution x ↦→ 14 − x. The sum of the first pair is 3 + 11 = 14. The sum of the second pair is 15 + 23 = 38 ≡ 14 (mod 24). The fixed points of this involution are 7 and 19, as established in Section 3.6. Thus, the four base steps are perfectly symmetric with respect to these two fixed points.

      3. The step 8+4 = 12. The transitions between these base steps alternate: 3+8 = 11;

      11 + 4 = 15; 15 + 8 = 23; 23 + 4 = 27 (which is 3 modulo 24). The cycle closes exactly after four steps, with a total displacement of 24 (a full octave).

      This closed cycle defines the chromatic filter: the base level of 24-TET resonates only with those inflation levels whose base steps belong to the set {3, 11, 15, 23}. All other base steps fall outside this resonance and do not synchronize directly with the chromatic pattern.


    7. The 353 Filter: A Shifted Symmetry

      The first level of inflation (3533353) exhibits an analogous—but shifted—filter. Empir-ical data show that 3533353 synchronizes only with patterns whose base steps form the following cycle:

      1, 5, 13, 17 (5)

      Once again, these four numbers reveal the same threefold symmetry:

      1. Tritone symmetry. The pair (1, 13) differs by 12. The pair (5, 17) also differs by

        12.

      2. Symmetry under shifted axes. The sum of the first pair is 1 + 13 = 14 (axis 7). The sum of the second pair is 5 + 17 = 22 (axis 11). Notably, 11 is itself a member of the chromatic filter {3, 11, 15, 23}.

      3. The step 4 + 8 = 12. The transitions alternate: 1 + 4 = 5; 5 + 8 = 13; 13 + 4 = 17;

      17 + 8 = 25 (which is 1 modulo 24). The cycle closes after four steps.

      This defines the 353 filter: {1, 5, 13, 17}.


    8. The 595 Filter: The Third Cycle

      The second level of inflation (5955595) has its own filter:

      7, 15, 19, 3 (6)

      1. Tritone symmetry. (7, 19) and (15, 3) differ by 12.

      2. Symmetry under shifted axes. 7 + 15 = 22; 19 + 3 = 22. The fixed points of the involution x ↦→ 22 − x are 11 and 23.

      3. The step 8 + 4 = 12. The cycle closes: 7 + 8 = 15; 15 + 4 = 19; 19 + 8 = 27 (3

      mod 24); 3 + 4 = 7.

      This defines the 595 filter: {7, 15, 19, 3}.


    9. The 7137 Filter: The Fourth Cycle

      The third level of inflation (713777137) has its own filter:

      9, 17, 21, 5 (7)

      1. Tritone symmetry. (9, 21) and (17, 5) differ by 12.

      2. Symmetry under shifted axes. 9 + 17 = 26 ≡ 2; 21 + 5 = 26 ≡ 2. The fixed points of the involution x ↦→ 26 − x are 1 and 13.

      3. The step 8 + 4 = 12. The cycle closes: 9 + 8 = 17; 17 + 4 = 21; 21 + 8 = 29 (5

      mod 24); 5 + 4 = 9.

      This defines the 7137 filter: {9, 17, 21, 5}.


    10. The Interlocking Architecture of Filters

      We have now identified four distinct filters:

      • Chromatic filter: {3, 11, 15, 23} — axes: 7, 19

      • 353 filter: {1, 5, 13, 17} — axes: 7, 11

      • 595 filter: {7, 15, 19, 3} — axes: 11, 23

      • 7137 filter: {9, 17, 21, 5} — axes: 1, 13 The interlocking pattern is now fully visible:

      • The chromatic filter contains 3 and 15; the 595 filter also contains 3 and 15.

      • The 353 filter contains 5 and 17; the 7137 filter also contains 5 and 17.

      • The axes interlock: the 353 filter’s axis 11 is a member of the chromatic filter; the 7137 filter’s axis 1 is a member of the 353 filter.

      Moreover, the axes form a cycle of their own: 7 → 11 → 23 → 13.


    11. The Complete Set of Odd Steps

      If we combine all four filters, we obtain the complete set of odd steps from 1 to 23:

      • Group A (Chromatic and 595): 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23

      • Group B (353 and 7137): 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21

      Together, these two groups cover every odd number in the 24-TET space. The sep-aration into two groups reflects the two interlocked 12-TET subsystems: Group A and Group B are the “even” and “odd” halves of the odd-step spectrum, each following the same 8-4-8-4 pattern, shifted by a constant.


    12. Connection to the Harmonic Sphere: Inflation and Modality

      The four filters identified in this chapter are not independent of the Harmonic Sphere. In fact, they are its direct expression in the dynamic domain.

      Recall that the Harmonic Sphere is parameterized by transposition k ∈ Z24 and mode

      m ∈ {0, 1}, where m = 0 corresponds to the direct mode S10 and m = 1 to the inverted

      10

      mode S′ . The inversion is given by the involution σ(x) = 14 − x.

      Now consider the four filters defined in the previous sections:

      • Filter A (chromatic): {3, 11, 15, 23}

      • Filter B (353): {1, 5, 13, 17}

      • Filter C (595): {7, 15, 19, 3}

      • Filter D (7137): {9, 17, 21, 5}

        Connection to the Harmonic Sphere: An Open Question

        The four filters identified in this chapter suggest a deep connection to the Harmonic Sphere. Recall that the Sphere is parameterized by the involution σ(x) = 14 − x, with fixed points 7 and 19.

        A preliminary inspection reveals that the filters form two pairs: (A, C) and (B, D). Furthermore, the sums of the pairs within each filter are related to the axes of the Sphere:

      • In Filter A: 3 + 11 = 14 and 15 + 23 = 38 ≡ 14 (mod 24). Both pairs sum to the

        axis 14.

      • In Filter D: 9 + 17 = 26 ≡ 2 and 21 + 5 = 26 ≡ 2 (mod 24). Both pairs sum to 2.

      This suggests that the filters are not arbitrary sets, but are constrained by the same symmetries that govern the Sphere. However, a direct mapping of the filters under the involution does not hold. For example, applying σ to Filter B yields:

      σ({1, 5, 13, 17}) = {13, 9, 1, 21} = {1, 9, 13, 21},

      which is not Filter D ({9, 17, 21, 5}).

      The precise algebraic relationship between the inflation filters and the mode inversion

      of the Sphere remains an open problem, to be addressed in future work. What is clear is that the dynamic network of intersections is deeply intertwined with the static geometry of the Sphere, even if the exact correspondence is more subtle than a simple involution.


    13. Conclusion: The Inflation Network

      The empirical data and the filter architecture reveal that the inflation network is not a random collection of patterns but a hierarchical, self-similar structure. The base level (chromatic) acts as a gatekeeper, admitting only four specific branches into direct syn-chronization. Each subsequent level refines the selection while preserving the underlying symmetries.

      The key findings of this section are:

      1. The inflation network is periodic. Synchronization patterns repeat every 24 steps.

      2. There are two regimes: slow (50 sync points) and fast (75–76 sync points). The fast regime occurs only at shifts of +4 and +10.

      3. Each level of inflation has its own filter, defined by a closed cycle of four base steps with transitions alternating +8 and +4.

      4. The filters interlock, sharing base steps and axes of symmetry.

      5. Together, the filters cover all odd steps, dividing them into two groups that correspond to the two 12-TET subsystems.

      6. The filters are the modes of the Harmonic Sphere, connected by the involu-tion x ↦→ 14 − x.

      This architecture is the generative engine of the Harmonic Lattice. It explains why the lattice is not a uniform grid but a selective, interlocking structure, and it provides a systematic method for navigating the 24-TET space through inflation.


  6. Conclusion

    This paper has developed the Harmonic Lattice: a compositional system for 24TET that extends the navigational framework of the Harmonic Compass [1] and the geometric framework of the Harmonic Sphere [2] into a complete tonal language.

    The principal findings are:

    1. The Harmonic Compass is a pair of rings (E, O) partitioning Z24, with a free and transitive action of Z12 on the rotated odd ring.

    2. Every harmonic lattice admits three distinct repetition rules: base (L0), overlap (L1), and concatenation (L2).

    3. The principal lattice L2(3, 5) is locally diatonic and globally chromatic.

    4. Every stretched lattice projects onto all 24 pairs of the compasses of its own steps.

    5. The map x ↦→ 14 − x is an involution with two fixed points, 7 and 19, the poles of the compass symmetry.

      10

    6. The modes S10 and S′ generate an amplituhedron-like structure that provides a

      combinatorial template for building lattices.

    7. Chord cascades are sequences of chords related by anchor-bridge embedding rela-tions.

    8. The anchor-bridge embedding operator Ep,q generates the cascade through iterated refinement, making harmony and voice leading two views of the same structural process.

    9. The Harmonic Lattice includes a dynamic network of intersections (the Inflation Network), which defines the rules of harmonic inflation. This network reveals that synchronization with the base level is governed by four interlocking filters, which reveal deep structural symmetries related to the direct and inverted modes of the Harmonic Sphere.

    The Harmonic Lattice is offered as both a theoretical framework and a compositional instrument. By integrating the Inflation Network, the Lattice not only provides a static map of pitch classes but also a dynamic mechanism for moving between them, fully bridging the compositional rules of the Lattice with the geometric structure of the Sphere.


  7. Future Work

Several directions remain open.

  1. General theory of universal projection. A general theorem characterizing the class of pairs (a, b) for which universal projection holds remains open.

  2. Periods of rotation paths. The periods T (d) = 24/ gcd(14+d, 24) of the rotation paths that arise from ring addition form a family of structures {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24}. Their relation to the anchor-bridge levels of the cascade is not yet fully understood.

  3. Higher-rank lattices. A natural extension is to lattices built from triples (a, b, c)

    or higher-rank structures.

  4. Perceptual studies. Controlled listener studies are needed to determine whether the midpoint bridge and asymmetric anchor levels are perceptually distinct.

  5. Extension to other temperaments. The framework is formulated in terms that do not depend on the specific division number 24.

  6. Compositional applications. The cascade framework can serve as the basis for algorithmic composition.

  7. Spectral analysis of cascades. The relation between the embedding types of a cascade and its spectral content remains to be developed.

Observation A.1. All block sums S are even, because S = b + 3a with a, b odd.

Observation A.2. The values S mod 24 cover all even residues from 0 to 22. The system is complete.

Observation A.3. Spiral lattices (8 in total) have S mod 24 ∈ {2, 10, 14, 22} and always

have cardinality 24.

Observation A.4. Closed lattices (2 in total) have S = 24 exactly and cardinality 4.

Observation A.5. Different lattices L(a, b) may share the same block sum S, and therefore the same closure period and linear closure, while differing in spectral content due to the order of steps.

‌Afterword


So, at this stage we can record the beginning of the construction of a tonal system for 24-TET; I am confident that compositional practice will help reveal its sound. At every stage of building the modes, a multitude of ideas visited me — and I am sure the reader has had their own unique ones as well, I even left some spaces as a hint here and there in the text in case of sudden insights; I look forward to your feedback.
